messages.subject: Re: Fixing factor loadings of fixing variances of latent factors
parts:
Any scaling method is arbitrary, including the "non-arbitrary" effects-coding method.  Here is an informative article on the topic:

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2018.1517356

The lavaan forum is for questions about the software.  General SEM questions can be posted on SEMNET:

https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?SUBED1=semnet&A=1

But if you are interested in the effects-coding method, lavaan has implemented it.  See the effect.coding description on the ?lavOptions help page.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Fixing factor loadings of fixing variances of latent factors
parts: the article gives a good overview

I agree it does, and the first author writes very well about technical issues in a nontechnical manner. But as the proponents of the effects-coding method, I think they (especially the first author) provided too rosy a picture of it, as evidenced by the title.  The article by Kloessner & Klopp also provides an excellent overview, and goes further to provide correct interpretations of a parameter across ID methods, which illuminate why the ID methods are ultimately arbitrary.

It's also true that the SEMnet is a better place for general questions. But I think we both know that there is a good chance that the discussion on SEMnet will unfortunately quickly move in a completely different direction.

Yes, Lesifer unfortunately poisons that otherwise very nourishing well of information. But he tends to only chime in on (and derail) discussions of model fit, despite how many times I have seen Keith Markus hand him his ass (not sure that American-ism translates well).  I try not to direct people to SEMNET for discussions of fit, since the tone quickly becomes predictably toxic, and I don't think this thread is one of the topics that would have led to more bad than good.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
